clinicalPearls: A rare inherited disorder of selective susceptibility to a specific group of beta-genus human papillomaviruses, usually autosomal recessive through defects in EVER1/TMC6, EVER2/TMC8, or CIB1
The skin shows widespread flat wart-like papules and reddish or hypopigmented, pityriasis-versicolor-like scaly macules, typically beginning in childhood
Lesions favour sun-exposed skin such as the face, neck, trunk, and limbs and persist rather than resolving as ordinary warts do
The major long-term hazard is the development of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in sun-exposed lesions during adulthood
Susceptibility is characteristically confined to these beta-papillomaviruses, so patients generally handle other infections normally in the classic (non-syndromic) form
A syndromic form occurs when the same skin phenotype arises secondarily in patients with T-cell immunodeficiency, in whom broader infection susceptibility is present
Management centres on rigorous photoprotection, surveillance and treatment of skin cancers, and lesion-directed dermatological therapy rather than a curative immunological treatment
reference.pathophysiology: In the classic form, loss-of-function mutations in EVER1/TMC6 or EVER2/TMC8, or in their partner CIB1, disrupt a keratinocyte protein complex that normally restricts the replication of beta-genus human papillomaviruses within skin cells, in part by regulating intracellular zinc handling. Without this intrinsic keratinocyte defence, these otherwise poorly pathogenic beta-papillomaviruses replicate unchecked in the epidermis, producing the persistent flat warts and versicolor-like macules. Because the defect is largely confined to keratinocyte control of these particular viruses rather than a global immune failure, susceptibility is narrowly restricted to beta-papillomaviruses. Chronic viral infection combined with ultraviolet exposure drives keratinocyte genomic damage over years, explaining the marked risk of squamous cell carcinoma on sun-exposed skin. In the syndromic form, an underlying T-cell immunodeficiency, rather than a keratinocyte-intrinsic defect, permits the same beta-papillomavirus disease alongside wider infection.
additionalDifferentials: Common viral warts (verruca vulgaris and plana)
Widespread warts in acquired immunosuppression such as HIV or transplantation
Syndromic epidermodysplasia verruciformis due to an underlying T-cell defect (for example GATA2, DOCK8, or other combined immunodeficiency)
Actinic keratoses and other photodamage lesions
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing characteristic histology with vacuolated keratinocytes
Human papillomavirus typing of lesions to identify beta-genus types
Genetic sequencing of TMC6, TMC8, and CIB1
Assessment of T-cell number and function to distinguish the syndromic form
Screening for HIV and other secondary immunosuppression
Regular dermatological surveillance with biopsy of suspicious lesions
Lymphocyte subset analysis where a combined immunodeficiency is suspected
redFlags: New, enlarging, ulcerated, or bleeding lesions suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Onset of the phenotype alongside features of broader immunodeficiency (pointing to the syndromic form)
Rapid lesion spread or unusually severe disease
Development of skin cancer at a young age
Extensive disease in a patient with unexplained recurrent infection
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy in the classic form is largely determined by the risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, which is high on sun-exposed skin from early adulthood; with strict photoprotection and vigilant surveillance many cancers are caught early, whereas the syndromic form carries the additional prognosis of the underlying immunodeficiency.
pitfalls: Dismissing persistent flat warts and versicolor-like macules as ordinary warts or tinea
Failing to institute lifelong photoprotection and skin-cancer surveillance
Missing an underlying T-cell immunodeficiency in the syndromic form
Assuming systemic immune treatment will clear the lesions in the classic keratinocyte-intrinsic form
Under-recognising the malignancy risk and delaying biopsy of changing lesions
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: With no curative antiviral therapy available, centre management on strict lifelong photoprotection using high-factor sunscreen and protective clothing to limit ultraviolet-driven carcinogenesis
Institute regular dermatological surveillance with a low threshold to biopsy any changing or suspicious lesion for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Treat wart-like lesions with topical agents such as retinoids, imiquimod or fluorouracil, cryotherapy or photodynamic therapy, accepting frequent recurrence
Excise or destroy cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas promptly, and consider systemic retinoids such as acitretin for extensive disease or chemoprevention
In the syndromic form, address the underlying T-cell immunodeficiency and minimise iatrogenic immunosuppression where feasible
Offer genetic counselling for this usually autosomal recessive condition, with testing of at-risk relatives
Refer to a multidisciplinary team spanning dermatology, clinical immunology and clinical genetics for long-term care
